passage:
Mohit, your mother says you kept repeating one joke at dinner. Let me tell you about me. I'm Aparna, and at nine I found a burp joke I thought was the funniest thing in the world. I told it to my class, my cousins, the milkman and my Nani, ten times in one day.
By the sixth, my cousin Rashi groaned, "We know!" I didn't stop. By the ninth, the milkman only nodded politely. But my Nani said, "It works better if you wait. Let them ask for it."
Next morning I waited until Rashi was bored and said, "Want to hear something gross?" She said yes. That was when I understood timing and audience.

qa.q: How many times did Aparna tell the joke on the first day?
qa.a: Aparna told the joke ten times in one day.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling as she kept telling the joke even after Rashi groaned?
qa.a: Aparna was excited and amused by her own joke, so pleased with it that Aparna could not stop even when others were bored.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Aparna told the joke?
qa.a: Nani told Aparna it works better to wait and let people ask for it. Aparna then waited until Rashi was bored and asked if she wanted to hear something gross.

qa.q: What did the groans and polite nods tell Rashi and the milkman about how they felt about the joke?
qa.a: They showed Rashi was tired of hearing it, and the milkman was being polite. The groans were honest feedback that the joke had been repeated too often.

grounding: A child repeats the same bodily joke ten times, and groans from listeners teach timing and audience.

passage:
The school bus had been stuck in the rain for forty minutes, wipers thumping, thirty children squashed together. Bhupen, eleven, stood up in the aisle. "Okay, okay, what did the toilet say to the toilet paper?"
"We've heard it," said Nirmala from the next seat, without looking up.
"You haven't heard THIS version." He told it, with a burp at the end.
Half the bus groaned. Nirmala said, "Bhupen. Third time today."
He sat down, a bit red. Then he leaned over. "What if I did it quieter, only for the back row? They haven't heard it yet."
"That could work," said Nirmala, and she smiled for the first time since they'd stopped.
He told it in a low voice to the back row, and they laughed.

qa.q: How long had the school bus been stuck in the rain?
qa.a: It had been stuck for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the half of the bus groaned and Nirmala said it was the third time?
qa.a: Bhupen felt embarrassed and a little deflated, going red. He wanted the laugh he expected.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that turned the groans into useful feedback?
qa.a: Bhupen adjusted his joke to a smaller audience, telling it quietly to the back row who had not heard it. He listened to the groans and changed.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt about hearing the same joke again on a long, wet ride?
qa.a: Nirmala was probably tired and fed up, as her reply shows, but she smiled when Bhupen listened and found a fix.

grounding: A child repeats the same toilet joke and learns from listeners' groans to adjust his timing and audience.

passage: The bus to Chacha's wedding in Nashik had been stuck in traffic for ninety minutes, the fan was broken, and everyone was sweaty and cross. Lakshmi, nine, decided this was the perfect time for her new joke. "Knock knock." Her cousin Rekha sighed. "Who's there?" "Burp." "Burp who?" "BURRRP!" Lakshmi collapsed with laughter. Rekha groaned. Lakshmi told it again. And again. By the sixth time Rekha put her dupatta over her face. By the eighth, the old man across the aisle was shaking his head. Lakshmi stopped. She looked around. Then she waited until the bus finally lurched forward, leaned over, and whispered the joke to the driver's little boy at the front instead. He howled. Lakshmi grinned. "See? It's the right person that matters," she told Rekha. "And not the ninth time."

qa.q: How long had the bus been stuck in traffic?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi thinking when she stopped and looked around after the eighth time?
qa.a: She seemed to realise, a little embarrassed, that her joke had stopped working on this tired audience.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi learn about telling jokes?
qa.a: That the right listener and timing matter, and that groans are a sign to stop or change the audience.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel by the sixth time?
qa.a: Rekha was fed up, putting her dupatta over her face.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a bodily joke many times and learning about timing and audience from her listeners' groans.

passage: At dinner in their Andheri flat, Ojas, eight, cleared his throat. "Why did the elephant sit on the toilet?" His sister Sarika, thirteen, put down her roti. "Ojas, we're eating." "Because it needed a BIG—" "OJAS." Papa hid a smile behind his glass. Ojas told the joke again anyway, louder. Sarika groaned and left for the kitchen. Ojas looked at the empty chair, then at Papa, then at Nani, who was chewing very slowly with her eyes twinkling. The next evening, when Sarika wasn't around, Ojas tried it on Nani alone. She laughed so hard she had to wipe her eyes. After that, the elephant joke became Ojas and Nani's secret. At dinner, he told Sarika a joke about a flying samosa instead, and she actually snorted.

qa.q: Who laughed so hard she had to wipe her eyes?
qa.a: Nani laughed so hard she had to wipe her eyes.

qa.q: What was Ojas thinking when he looked at Sarika's empty chair?
qa.a: He seemed a little disappointed and puzzled, starting to notice that his joke had driven his sister away.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saving the toilet joke for Nani and telling Sarika the samosa joke worked, because he matched each joke to the person who would enjoy it.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Ojas's joke at dinner?
qa.a: She finds it gross and annoying at the table, so she groans and leaves.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a toilet joke, using the groans and laughter of different listeners to learn about timing and audience.

passage:
"Devika, Devika, what do you call a cow with no legs?"
"Tejas, you told me this yesterday."
"Ground beef!"
"Also yesterday."
"Okay, okay, new one. Why did the boy bring toilet paper to the party?"
Devika narrowed her eyes. "Why?"
"Because he was a PARTY POOPER!"
Devika groaned so loudly the dinner lady turned around. Then she laughed anyway. "That's so gross."
"But you laughed!"
"Only the first time. If you say it again, I'm not laughing."
Tejas thought about this. "So I only get one go?"
"One go. Then find someone new."
Tejas grinned and ran towards the Class 4 table. "Arjun! Why did the boy bring toilet paper—"
Devika shook her head, smiling. 😄

qa.q: What did Devika say she would do if Tejas told the joke again?
qa.a: She said, 'If you say it again, I'm not laughing.'

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when Devika laughed at the party joke?
qa.a: He felt delighted and proud, shouting 'But you laughed!' because his new joke landed.

qa.q: How did Devika's feedback help Tejas?
qa.a: Her groan, then laugh, then 'one go' rule taught him that a joke works once per listener, so he took it to a new audience.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had laughed at every repeat?
qa.a: Tejas might never learn about timing or fresh audiences, and might keep repeating the same joke.

grounding: Shows a child testing toilet jokes on a friend and using her groans as feedback about timing and audience.

passage: Last year I found the best joke in the world. I'm Dolma, and the joke was: "Why did the toilet paper roll down the hill? To get to the bottom!" I told it to Ama at breakfast. I told it to the bus driver. I told it to Lokesh at lunch, then again in the line. By the tenth time, Lokesh groaned so loudly the whole line turned round. Nobody laughed. My face went hot. That evening I tried it on my baby cousin, who laughs at everything, so that didn't count. Then I changed my plan. I waited until Lokesh burped in assembly and whispered, "Excuse you, the bottom's that way." He snorted so hard he had to step out. Timing, I learned. Not ten times.

qa.q: Who did Dolma tell the joke to at breakfast?
qa.a: Dolma told it to Ama at breakfast.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when nobody laughed the tenth time?
qa.a: Dolma felt embarrassed, face going hot, when Lokesh groaned and the whole line turned round.

qa.q: What did Dolma learn from the groans?
qa.a: That a joke needs the right moment and a fresh audience, not ten repeats, so Dolma waited for a fitting moment 😅

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt hearing the joke for the tenth time?
qa.a: He was probably bored and a bit irritated, which is why he groaned so loudly.

grounding: Shows a child testing a toilet joke over and over and using listeners' groans to learn about timing and audience.
